Federal Courts. The system of courts established under the United States Constitution to interpret federal law and resolve disputes involving federal issues. Headed by the Supreme Court, the federal judiciary serves as a co-equal branch alongside the executive and legislative branches, wielding the power of judicial review.

The federal courts are established by Article Three of the Constitution, which creates the Supreme Court and authorizes Congress to create lower federal courts as needed to handle federal business. They operate separately from state court systems; federal courts hear cases involving federal law, interstate disputes, constitutional questions, and disputes between states. They include district courts, which are trial courts with fact-finding jurisdiction; courts of appeals, which are appellate courts reviewing district decisions; and specialized courts such as bankruptcy, tax, and patent courts. The Supreme Court serves as the ultimate arbiter of constitutional interpretation, with decisions binding on all lower courts and fundamentally shaping American governance. The federal courts gained power to declare laws unconstitutional through Marbury v. Madison in eighteen oh-three, establishing judicial review, a transformative power that made courts co-equal with legislatures. They are limited by the requirement of standing, meaning plaintiffs must demonstrate concrete injury, and justiciability doctrines that prevent advisory opinions and limit courts to actual cases or controversies. Appointment of federal judges is controlled by the President with Senate confirmation, shaping jurisprudence across generations; federal judges serve for life during good behavior. Federal courts can overturn state laws that violate federal law or the Constitution, making them instruments of national authority over state legislatures. They serve as final arbiter of constitutional disputes, and their interpretation of the Constitution effectively amends it without formal amendment, giving the judiciary immense power. The federal courts connect to the United States Supreme Court as the apex of the federal court system; the judicial branch as the constitutional branch that federal courts comprise; the principle of separation of powers by which courts check executive and legislative power; Marbury v. Madison which established the courts' power of judicial review; constitutional law as the primary domain of federal judicial interpretation; judicial review as the transformative power the federal courts wield; and Baker v. Carr which exemplifies federal courts resolving apportionment questions.
